title: Morse Code Translator
story: Before the internet, before telephones, there was Morse code — dots and dashes tapped across telegraph wires spanning continents. A single operator could send 'SOS' (... --- ...) and summon rescue ships across an ocean. Now YOU build the translator. Type any word, hear it in dots and dashes. Receive a string of beeps, decode it back to English. Two centuries of communication history, running in your code.
why: The Morse Code Translator exercises Map for lookup tables, string iteration/construction, bidirectional encoding/decoding, and character validation — a complete encoding system that demonstrates data transformation patterns.
analogy: A telegraph operator's cheat sheet pinned to the wall: A is .- (dot-dash), B is -... (dash-dot-dot-dot). Encoding means looking up each letter on the sheet and tapping it out. Decoding means listening to the taps and finding the matching letter. Your Map is that cheat sheet, and your functions are the operator's trained fingers and ears.
try_it: Add support for punctuation: . = .-.-.-, , = --..--, ? = ..--.., ! = -.-.--. Add a 'sound' simulation that prints 'BEEP' for dots and 'BEEEEP' for dashes. Add word separation: two spaces between words in morse. Build a function that accepts a full sentence ('HELLO WORLD') and encodes space as '/' between words.
tips: Map.get() returns Option — use unwrap_or("?") for unknown characters
Reverse map is built by iterating all known letters and swapping key/value: code→letter
Morse tokens are separated by single spaces, words by double spaces — handle both
common_mistakes: Forgetting uppercase — Morse alphabet is uppercase; lowercase 'a' won't match 'A'
Building the reverse map by hand — it's error-prone; derive it programmatically from the forward map
Not handling spaces correctly during decode — a single space means next letter, double space means next word
